manifest.name: dsh-taskfold
manifest.description: Keeps long coding-agent sessions lean: wrap a stretch of work in a named task, and when it ends, fold that whole span into one short titled summary. The conversation stays readable, context costs stay low, and any fold's original content can be read back on demand. Built for DeepSeek Harness.
manifest.author: yindf

scripts.test: node test/task-marks.test.mjs && node test/fold-drain.test.mjs && node test/span-preview.test.mjs && node test/taskfold-stats.test.mjs && node test/release.test.mjs && node test/fold-engine.test.mjs && node test/fold-instruction.test.mjs...

bundle.text:
# taskfold bundle patch: registers the taskfold tool family (task_begin /
# task_end / list_folds / fold_recall) at the host plane (profile bundle
# layer). Tools land in the global tools registry — every session of every
# preset sees them.
#
# ONE host row + ONE browser row = two components on the Plugins page. The
# observation tools (list_folds / fold_recall) used to be a second host row
# (`cmpct-stats`); they are now a plain module registered by taskfold.mjs, so
# removing that row loses nothing — only the component count drops. The
# browser half can never share the host row: client-modules discovers a
# client package from a live Loader row, and two rows of ONE package make it
# throw "resolves from multiple active Loader sources" — hence the nested
# client package with this row as its single owner.
#
# Row ids (taskfold / taskfold-client) are the component names the Plugins
# page shows. The FIRST id is also the CONFIG KEY of this row's Settings form
# (dsh-settings keys a form by entry id), so renaming it a second time would
# orphan a saved fold floor; treat it as stable from here on.
#
# HOST ROW SPECIFIER: the package SUBPATH 'dsh-taskfold/plugins', never
# './plugins/taskfold.mjs'. A './…' row name is rewritten into a file:/// URL
# before the Plugins page reads it, and dsh-app-boot's readPluginMeta() bails
# out on every specifier that carries no package name (barePackageName() ===
# undefined) — the row would then render that raw path with no title,
# description or icon. The subpath resolves through the profile's own
# node_modules (the `dsh plugin add` link) into this package's exports map,
# and readPluginMeta() reads `<specifier>/locale/*.json` plus
# `<specifier>/package.json`: plugins/locale/*.json carries this row's title
# Taskfold and its one-line introduction, while plugins/package.json — the
# description fallback — is deliberately absent and unexported, so the row's
# copy can only come from that locale. package.json + the package-level
# locale/*.json keep the longer blurb for the package page header and npm. exports["."] and
# exports["./plugins"] name the same module.
#
# CLIENT ROW SPECIFIER: this component's OWN package name, mounted exactly the
# way the official bundles mount their halves (@deepseek-ai/
# dsh-experimental-agent-team-profile declares one resolvable package per
# component and each carries its own locale/*.json). Two host rules meet here.
# client-modules' locatePkgJson() accepts a row name only when it is path-like
# OR an exact bare package name — every other specifier (a subpath of the root
# package, notably) is dropped outright, taking the browser half with it. And
# readPluginMeta() can title a row only through a package name: boot rewrites a
# './…' row name into a file:/// URL, so a relative name renders as that raw
# path. A bare name satisfies both. It resolves because this package.json
# declares it and dsh-app-boot publishes a profile bundle's resolvable
# dependencies as scope:'profile' resolution entries (profile.ts:
# collectProfileScopePackages -> dependencyClosure, walking the bundle
# manifest's dependencies/peers); the row then loads client/index.mjs, and
# readPluginMeta() reads client/locale/*.json plus client/package.json —
# whose own description stays absent, so the row's copy can only come from the
# locale. Both row locales carry a title and ONE short introduction, and both
# titles are deliberately distinct from their row id and module name: client.js
# prints the id only when the title differs from it, and the module name only
# when the title differs from that, so each row renders the same four lines
# (title, introduction, id, module) — the shape the official bundles use.
#
# The compaction engine resolves LAZILY inside the plugin and is ALWAYS the
# plugin's own ScopedEngine (span-scoped summarizer; auto:false; imported on
# demand — bare specifier first, then a file-URL fallback walking up from
# host anchors). A realm-registered engine, if any, is left to serve AUTO
# compaction. No compaction row is required here.
#
# COLLISION WARNING: never mount this bundle alongside a preset that already
# carries its own taskfold-era rows (the historical cmpct-region /
# cmpct-stats ids, e.g. the cmpct agent preset) — tool names live in a shared
# registry and duplicate registration fails.
- insert:
    - id: taskfold
      name: 'dsh-taskfold/plugins'

    # Dedicated owner row of the browser bundle: the nested client package,
    # mounted by its own name. client-modules maps each client package (a
    # package.json declaring dsh.client) to its Loader rows and refuses a
    # package with more than one active source ("resolves from multiple active
    # Loader sources"), which is exactly what a second row over the root
    # package would do. This row is that package's single owner (empty host
    # apply; the browser half does all the work). See CLIENT ROW SPECIFIER
    # above for why the name — not a path — is what makes the row both load
    # and render with a title.
    - id: taskfold-client
      name: 'dsh-taskfold-client'

readme.text:
effectively infinite context for your coding agent

简体中文 · Releases · Changelog

Keep long AI coding sessions fast, cheap, and readable: finished work is folded into a short summary, and the full original content is always one call away.

For [DeepSeek Harness](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/dsh) (DSH).

> **Latest supported dsh: `0.2.1-rc.5`.** dsh rc builds are supported on this branch; dsh alpha builds are supported on the [`alpha` branch](https://github.com/yindf/taskfold/blob/alpha/README.md#supported-dsh-versions).
That dialog does the same thing as the command line below: it writes the dependency and the bundle entry into the active profile (`desktop` for dsh Desktop). Nothing else needs configuring by hand.

`dsh plugin --profile <name> add` is the shell equivalent of the dialog. `desktop` is dsh Desktop's profile and `web` is the DSH Web GUI's — use whichever one you actually run:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile desktop add dsh-taskfold

readme.section: a pinned version — required while the release is younger than 24 h; 0.37.7/0.38.0 cannot be installed
readme.text: dsh plugin --profile desktop add dsh-taskfold@<version>

readme.section: a channel branch (keep the quotes: # starts a comment in sh)
readme.text:
dsh plugin --profile web add "github:yindf/taskfold#master"
dsh plugin --profile web add "github:yindf/taskfold#alpha"
```

Whichever way you install, restart dsh afterwards.

readme.section: Channels, the npm package, and support
readme.text: [`dsh-taskfold`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-taskfold) on npm is a **prebuilt** package — it skips dsh's `allowBuilds` build approval, and since 0.37.6 the release pipeline publishes it for the **rc channel** (`master`) only: the alpha channel's releases ship as GitHub Releases and never reach npm. The bare name therefore follows the rc channel's newest release; pin `@version` for determinism, or enter the branch's Git address.

readme.section: Channels, the npm package, and support
readme.text:
`master` carries the rc channel and `alpha` carries the alpha channel: this branch records the rc channel's support range (see [Supported dsh versions](#supported-dsh-versions)) and the alpha channel's record lives on the [alpha branch](https://github.com/yindf/taskfold/blob/alpha/README.md#supported-dsh-versions).

Restart dsh — every session on that profile gets the tools. The agent then wraps its work in named tasks:

readme.section: Channels, the npm package, and support
readme.text:
```
task_begin("fix the login bug")   … the work …   task_end("fix the login bug")
```

and that whole span collapses into one titled summary, still readable back with `fold_recall`.

Long sessions drown in their own history: every request re-sends hours of finished work — old tool outputs, debug logs, abandoned attempts. Costs climb, the model gets distracted, and eventually the context window fills up.

taskfold fixes this the way a good notebook does. While working, the agent wraps each task with `task_begin("fix the login bug")`. When the task is done, `task_end` closes it **and** replaces the entire back-and-forth with a short titled summary:

```
Before:  [800 messages of raw debugging…]
After:   "fix the login bug" — summary: what was tried, what failed and why,
          what changed, what the user decided. (~1 screen)
```

The conversation stays readable, every request gets cheaper, and the model keeps the *lessons* without dragging the *transcript* along.
**Nothing is lost.** Every fold saves the exact original messages to a file, and `fold_recall({ fold: N })` can regenerate it at any time. Fold first, look later — like closing a book you can reopen.

readme.section: How it relates to dsh's built-in compaction
readme.text:
- **dsh's built-in compaction is automatic and pressure-driven.** It fires when the window is nearly full, picks a range by token pressure, and replaces it with a summary; the original events stay in the session log, shadowed rather than deleted.
- **taskfold is explicit and task-scoped.** You fold each finished task as you go, so the summary is written while its span is still in context — accurate by construction — and it is titled, so the session stays navigable.
- **Because you fold early, the window rarely fills.** In the measured session below the peak was 20.7% instead of 59.5%, so pressure compaction fires later, or not at all — and when it does fire, there is less left to summarize.
- **Every fold is addressable.** `fold_recall({ fold: N })` returns the exact original messages, not a re-summary.

- **Named tasks.** The agent opens a task before starting work and closes it when done. Open tasks survive restarts; closing is well-ordered (innermost first), and a failed close never corrupts anything — just retry.
- **Folding = closing + summarizing in one call.** The summary is written once, while the original span is still in context, so it's accurate — not a "summary of a summary".
- **Summaries keep what matters.** The summarizer is instructed to preserve user decisions and feedback (verbatim where wording matters), pitfalls and *why* things failed, what changed, and the outcome.
- **Gentle guardrails.** If the agent forgets the discipline, a short hint appears in its context. Hints are events, not state: one is published only when the condition appears or its wording changes, nothing is published once the condition clears (the model already complied and does not need to be told), and there is no wrapper, supersession header, or expiry notice — no noise when the flow is healthy.
- **Cheap on the cache.** Folding only rewrites a middle chunk of history; the stable prefix (system prompt, tools, earlier context) stays cache-friendly.

One real session — 411 model steps, 26 folds — read from the harness's own usage records:

| | Without folding | With taskfold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total prompt tokens | 142,654,308 | 52,127,098 (**−63.5%**) |
| Largest single request | 594,909 | 206,896 (−65%) |
| Context window used at peak | 59.5% | 20.7% |

The mechanism: folding moved **441,100 tokens** of finished work off the surface. Because that history would otherwise be re-sent on every later request, it added up to **90,527,210 tokens never sent**. Producing the 26 summaries cost 3,550,270 tokens (3.9% of the saving, and most of it cache reads); the biggest single fold took 40,422 tokens out of the conversation in one call.

Most of those tokens would have been cache *reads* rather than fresh input — cheaper, but still billed and still occupying the window. In longer sessions that is the difference between staying inside the context window and not.

One session, one task shape — your numbers will differ. The mechanism is the point: finished work leaves the surface, the stable prefix stays cached, and the model keeps the lessons instead of the transcript.

Four agent tools (plus the reminders above):

| Tool | One-liner |
| --- | --- |
| `task_begin({ name })` | Open a named task. |
| `task_end({ name })` | Close it and fold its whole span into one titled summary. |
| `list_folds` | List all folds (number, size, title). |
| `fold_recall({ fold })` | Bring back any fold's original content on demand. |

In the Web GUI, the current open-task stack can also show as a live dock above the composer (like the todo panel) — hidden by default, switched on with `showTaskBar` on the Plugins page: outermost first, the innermost task highlighted, with the closing/pending counts — read straight from the session's `taskMarks` projection, no extra events.

Folding has one user-configurable lower bound, set on the host's **Plugins page** as a "Taskfold" card (the browser half registers it while the Host serves the taskfold namespace — no environment variables, no restart):

- **`minSpanTokens`** (default `2000`) — the minimum number of estimated tokens a closed task's span must carry before it is worth a summarization call. The count is a CJK-aware character heuristic over the span's message text, taken before any model call (its rate constants are calibrated against measured `shadowedTokenCount` values; estimates read ~7% low, a conservative direction). A span below the floor closes **unfolded, and the verdict is made at close time and recorded in the `Task ended` result itself** (0.37.6): the span never enters the archival queue, so the skip is permanent by construction — no reopen path exists, because retro-folding settled spans would rewrite the surface and invalidate the provider prefix cache behind them, a cost no small fold can repay. Closes whose carrying message also calls other tools (their partner results have not landed when `task_end` executes) fall back to drain-time, in-memory settling, re-measured after a restart. `0` folds everything; an unmeasurable span always folds. Invalid values (non-integer, negative) fall back to the default, never throw. Edits are validated by the form's schema, persisted in the active profile's config, and ap

Every user-facing surface ships English and Simplified Chinese. The settings card resolves its copy through the host's locale service (dictionaries `settings.taskfold`). The task-stack dock's registration deliberately carries no locale requirement — the bundle wires a locale-bound reader for dictionary `ui.taskfold` while the locale service is available, and the dock prints its built-in English copy otherwise, so it renders on every deployment. The package also exports `locale/en.json` + `locale/zh.json` (the package page header and the npm listing) plus one row locale per mounted component — `plugins/locale/*.json` for the host row, reached through the subpath it mounts (`dsh-taskfold/plugins`), and `client/locale/*.json` for the client row, reached through its own package name (`dsh-taskfold-client`) — so the Plugins page shows each row's title and one-line introduction in the active language instead of the English `package.json` fallback. Both row titles deliberately differ from their row id and their module name: `client.js` prints the id only when the title differs from it and the module name only when the title differs from that, so each row renders the same four lines — titl

Every release attaches a prebuilt `dsh-taskfold-<version>.tgz`. Plugin storefronts offer that asset — or the npm package — instead of the build-from-source command, which also skips dsh's `allowBuilds` approval step — see the [latest release](https://github.com/yindf/taskfold/releases/latest).

- **rc channel — supported through `0.2.1-rc.5`** (verified 2026-10-30 — two patch steps with no host-surface change: the monorepo moved 0.2.1-rc.3 → 0.2.1-rc.5 (rc.4 shipped and was superseded the same day; this record verifies the cumulative rc.3 → rc.5 delta, and `latest` and `next` both now point at `0.2.1-rc.5`), and the `@deepseek-ai/*` closure is the **same 307-package set** — zero added, zero removed — with 297 version-locked to `0.2.1-rc.5` and the ten non-lockstep packages unmoved (`cordis 4.0.5`, the four `cordis-plugin-*`, `cosmokit 1.8.6`, `libreoffice-kit 0.1.5`, `node-addon-system 0.1.2`, `schemastery 3.18.5`). Per-file diffs of the 19 packages this plugin touches (excluding `.map`) show **17 changed only their `package.json` version and dependency pins**; the only real code deltas in that set are client-side — `dsh-client-ui-conversation` (each view-tab label now estimates its own glyph width and shows its full-name tooltip only when that estimate exceeds the 88px cell, and the More button no longer names the folded active View in its tooltip — that string was removed) and `dsh-client-modules` (its embedded commit stamp only) — while across the whole 307-package sur

- Layout: `plugins/` (ONE mounted host row, `taskfold.mjs` mounted as the package subpath `dsh-taskfold/plugins` — the bundle patch declares one host component, so the Plugins page shows two: this row and the client row, which is mounted by its own component package name `dsh-taskfold-client`; `compact-stats.mjs` is a plain module imported by it, not a row; plus the shared plain modules they import — `events.mjs`, `task-marks.mjs`, `fold-instruction.mjs`, `fold-engine.mjs`, `fold-drain.mjs`, `fold-settings.mjs`, `lifecycle-nudges.mjs`, `lifecycle-injection.mjs`, `span-preview.mjs`, plus the browser half: `task-stack-ui.mjs` — the dock's source of truth — and `fold-settings-ui.mjs` — the Plugins-page settings card, both generated into `client/taskfold-client.mjs` by `scripts/build-client.mjs`), `client/` (the nested `dsh-taskfold-client` package owning the browser bundle — a client package may have exactly ONE owning Loader row, and the host half already owns the root package row; it is **published as its own npm package** and the root declares it under `dependencies` as a registry version range, so dsh-app-boot's dependency closure publishes the name, the row mounts the bare name i

A star helps other dsh users find it — in this ecosystem, that is how a plugin gets discovered. Numbers from your own sessions are welcome in [Discussions](https://github.com/yindf/taskfold/discussions).
